To use verbs of feeling + que + subjunctive: me alegra que, me da pena que, me sorprende que, me molesta que, me emociona que.
To distinguish "me alegro de + infinitive" (same subject) from "me alegro de que + subjunctive" (different subjects).
To apply the sequence of tenses: present → present or perfect subjunctive (me alegro de que vengas / hayas venido); past → imperfect subjunctive (me alegré de que vinieras).
To express regret about something unreal: me habría gustado que + imperfect / pluperfect subjunctive; ojalá hubiera.

Friday, 23 April, Book Day, at El Mostrador in Madrid, an hour before the launch of the two books. Ecaterina and Marta are waiting at the back. Begoña walks in unexpectedly.
I'm a bundle of nerves. I'm surprised you're so calm.
I'm not calm. But this time the book isn't mine. I'm glad other people are doing the talking.

And I would have liked Andrés to see this. The letters, the queue, everything.
Good evening. Don't look at me like that. It's Book Day. Even I read.
Begoña! I'm so glad you came.
I find it strange that you find it strange. The cover of your novel is by my photographer.
And the last photo in her series is me. Thank you for putting me last.
Don't thank me. I hate being thanked. What matters about a series is how it ends.
So, are you staying for the launch?

"haya" is pronounced "a-ya", the "h" is silent and "y" is like a consonantal "i": A-yas-ve-NI-do. Don't confuse it with "allá" (a-YA).
The imperfect subjunctive in -ra: vi-NIE-ras, stressed on "nie". In the plural, the first person has a written accent: vi-NIÉ-ra-mos.
Two hard "g"s: gar-GAN-ta. "Nudo en la garganta" is joined: NU-doen-la-gar-GAN-ta.

With "gustar"-type verbs (me alegra, me sorprende, me molesta), the grammatical subject is the "que" clause. With "alegrarse de", you need "de": «Me alegro de que…».
2. Infinitive or que + subjunctive?
I'm glad to be here. (same subject → infinitive)
I'm glad you're here. (different subjects → subjunctive)
I'm sorry to be leaving.
I'm sorry you're leaving.
Typical mistake: "Me alegro que estás aquí". "De" and the subjunctive are missing. Correct: «Me alegro de que estés aquí».

The two books arrived from the printer on the same day, Wednesday, 14 April, in two boxes that Inés sent by courier to Bucharest and to Madrid. In Bucharest, Ecaterina opened hers on the living-room table, with the little lamp lit, as she had opened the box of "Lampa aprinsă" a year and a half earlier. Inside were ten copies of "Las cartas que no mandamos". There was no author's name on the cover, as she had asked, only the title and a photo by Andrei: an open wooden drawer full of envelopes. She opened the first copy at the endpapers. There they were, in very small print, the two hundred and twenty-eight names. Ecaterina read them all, one by one, under her breath.

It took her almost half an hour. When she finished, she realised she had a lump in her throat, and that it wasn't sadness, but something harder to name. She called Ana. She told her the book had arrived. Ana asked her what it was like. Ecaterina answered that she was very glad her name wasn't on the cover, because that way it was clear whose book it was. Ana asked her whether her name appeared anywhere. Ecaterina told her yes, at the end of the introduction, in small print, like a signature. Ana told her she was glad it was there at least. Ecaterina replied that it was fine there, at the end, like the last one to come in.

In Madrid, Marta opened her box in the flat on calle del Prado, alone, sitting on the hallway floor, because she didn't dare carry it to the table. "La librera de Triana" had Andrei's photo on the cover: Faustino's back walking away along the Cuesta de Moyano, with the red beret. Marta took out a copy, smelled it, opened it at the last page and read the last word, the one Faustino had suggested in his dictionary: "agradecimiento". Then she called Faustino in Triana. Faustino took a long time to answer. When he finally did, Marta told him the book had arrived. Faustino told her he already knew, that doña Remedios had given him goosebumps reading him the back cover.

Inés had organised the launch of the two books for Friday, 23 April, Book Day, at seven in the evening, at El Mostrador. It was the hardest date of the year to launch a book in Spain, because every bookshop was full, every street had stalls and every writer was signing at the same time. But Inés said there was no other possible date, that two books about letters and booksellers had to be born on the day of books. When Lola found out, she said El Mostrador was a café and not a bookshop, and that it couldn't hold more than sixty people. Inés replied that sixty would fit inside, then, and the rest would wait on calle de las Huertas.

Inés had done something else, without telling anyone. During March she had written to the two hundred and twenty-eight authors of the letters to invite them to the launch. She didn't expect many to come, because they lived all over Spain and some were very old. But forty-three replied. Forty-three people who had written a letter to a newspaper after reading an article, and who were going to travel to Madrid on Book Day to see their letter in a book. Inés told Ecaterina only a week before, on the phone. Ecaterina was silent for so long that Inés thought the call had dropped. Then she told her she was a bundle of nerves.

Ecaterina flew to Madrid on Wednesday the 21st. She didn't go alone. Ana had managed to get three days off at the Instituto Cervantes and had decided to take Rosa Elena, even if she had to miss two days of school; Mrs Ionescu had given permission on one condition: that when she got back, Rosa Elena would tell the club, in Spanish, everything she had seen. Mr Dan and his wife went too, because Mr Dan had said that, after two years of studying Spanish, he had no intention of missing the most Spanish day of the year. And at the last minute Elena, Mihai's mother, joined them; she had never been to Spain and said that at her age nothing frightened her any more, not even planes.

That same afternoon, as soon as they had left their bags at the hotel, Ecaterina took Elena and Rosa Elena to calle de las Huertas. Elena had never been outside Romania, except once to Bulgaria, in 1979, to the beach. She stood in front of the green sign with her handbag clutched to her chest, as if she were afraid someone would take it. Rosa Elena read her the plaque aloud, in Spanish, and then translated it into Romanian, word by word. Elena asked her who had taught her to read like that. Rosa Elena told her Mrs Ionescu, Grandma Ecaterina and a trucker. Elena told her she was surprised that a six-year-old girl had so many teachers. Rosa Elena answered that she wasn't.

Grandpa Gheorghe didn't go. He was ninety-seven and the village doctor had told him that a plane, at his age, was reckless. Grandpa didn't protest. He told Ecaterina he was sorry he couldn't go, but glad that everyone else was going. He asked for just one thing: that someone make him a video of the whole launch, from beginning to end, without cutting anything, so he could watch it on the porch with the lamp lit. Rosa Elena said she would do it, with her camera. Grandpa told her very well, but please, this time, not to film only the ceiling, as in the Christmas show video. Rosa Elena promised she wouldn't.

Costel couldn't go either. That week he had the Valencia run, and the boss couldn't change it again. But on Thursday the 22nd, when he reached Valencia, he went by Álex's school before going to Irina's, as always. The walnut tree was already almost ten centimetres tall. It had five leaves, small and of a green so light it looked unreal. Álex and three classmates were watering it when Costel arrived. Costel took a photo of the four of them around the walnut tree, with the green sign behind. Then he recorded a short video, in Spanish, for them to play at the launch. Álex helped him rehearse. They recorded it four times. Costel said he was more nervous than in the C1 exam.

On Thursday morning, Mr Dan asked to see the agency where his son worked. Andrei got nervous, because he had never taken his father to work, and because Begoña was in her office. Mr Dan walked in with his jacket buttoned and his notebook of "pairs" in his pocket. Begoña came out to greet him. They shook hands. Mr Dan told her, in very correct Spanish, that he was very pleased to meet her and thanked her for everything she had done for his son. Begoña answered that she hadn't done anything, that the boy had done it all himself. Then she showed him the photo of Ecaterina writing in Triana. Mr Dan looked at it for a long time. He said nothing. He had goosebumps.

Faustino and doña Remedios arrived from Seville on Thursday, on the AVE, with Curro and an enormous suitcase that was full not of clothes but of books: twenty copies of "La librera de Triana" that doña Remedios had bought in her own bookshop to give to the customers on the Cuesta de Moyano. Faustino was wearing his red beret and Rosa Elena's mărțișor still pinned to his lapel, although it was already April. When he got off the train at Atocha, he stood still on the platform for a moment, looking around. Doña Remedios asked him what was wrong. Faustino told her that seven months ago he had walked out of Madrid through this same station without looking back, and that now he found it strange that everything was still the same.

That evening they all had dinner at Marta's flat on calle del Prado: fourteen people in a living room that normally held six. Faustino finally met Mr Dan, and the two discovered they had something in common: neither of them could make a tortilla without it falling apart. Doña Remedios and Elena, who didn't have a single word in common, sat together on the sofa and spent an hour showing each other photos of their grandchildren on their phones, laughing, pointing, nodding. Ana, watching them from the kitchen, told Marta it moved her that two grandmothers could understand each other so well without speaking. Marta told her grandmothers had their own language, and it wasn't taught at any institute.

Book Day dawned sunny. In the morning, Faustino asked to be taken to the Cuesta de Moyano. Lucas had opened the stall at eight, although it was a Friday, because on 23 April all the stalls opened. When he saw Faustino coming up the slope, slowly, on doña Remedios's arm, in his red beret, Lucas stood for a moment not knowing what to do. Then he ran out of the stall, hugged him and said: "¡Quillo! How amazing that you've come!" Faustino told him he was glad the stall was still open. Lucas replied that he had promised him. That no way was he going to close it. And he offered him the stool. Faustino sat down.

He spent the whole morning there, sitting on his usual stool, signing copies of "La librera de Triana" as if the book were his. The regular customers recognised him at once: the retired teacher with the history books, the lady with her husband's library, the young man who was now a teacher in Vallecas. They all told him the same thing: that they were very glad he had come back, even if only for a day. And he gave them all the same answer: that he hadn't come back, he was visiting. Doña Remedios, sitting beside him on a folding chair, gave each of them a copy of the novel. When the twenty ran out, Lucas took more from Marta's box.

At midday Begoña appeared. Nobody was expecting her. She had the big camera over her shoulder and the black felt mărțișor, which she hadn't taken off since 1 March. She stopped in front of the stall and looked at Faustino sitting on the stool. Faustino looked at her. For a few seconds neither said anything. Then Faustino told her he hadn't seen her buy a book in thirty years. Begoña told him she had come to buy one. Faustino gave her a copy of Marta's novel and told her that one was free. Begoña told him nobody gave her anything for free. Faustino told her it wasn't a present, it was a debt from 1995. Begoña smiled.

Nobody ever found out what debt that was. Andrei, who was there, asked Faustino afterwards, but Faustino only told him that in 1995 a young photographer, just back from a war, had spent a whole afternoon at his stall without buying anything, looking at photography books, and that he had let her take one without paying, because it was obvious she needed it more than the money. Begoña had never paid him back. And she had never come back to the stall. Faustino told Andrei he was very glad that, thirty years later, Begoña had finally come back to pay her debt. Even if she did it by accepting a free book. Debts, he said, are paid however one can.

At half past six in the evening, calle de las Huertas was packed. It wasn't only because of the launch: on Book Day, the whole Barrio de las Letras filled with people carrying roses and books under their arms, because in Spain, on that day, it was traditional to give a rose and a book. But in front of El Mostrador there was a queue that reached the corner. Lola had brought out all the chairs, removed two tables and put Andrés's lamp in the middle, on the counter, lit. Next to it, on a small table, were the two new books, side by side: the one with the letters and the one about the bookseller. Lola glanced at them every two minutes, as if afraid they might run away.

Ecaterina and Marta had been waiting in the back room, behind the curtain, since six. Marta was a bundle of nerves. She told Ecaterina she was surprised she was so calm. Ecaterina answered that she wasn't calm, but that this time the book wasn't hers, and she was glad other people were doing the talking. Marta told her she was sorry Grandpa Gheorghe couldn't be there. Ecaterina told her she would have liked Andrés to see it: the letters, the queue, everything. At that moment the curtain opened. It was Begoña. The two of them stared at her. Begoña told them not to look at her like that, that it was Book Day, and even she read.

At seven o'clock sharp the launch began. Inés spoke first, very briefly. She said that tonight the authors on the cover weren't going to speak, but the authors of the letters. And then, one by one, some of the forty-three who had come stepped up into the small space in front of the counter. Joaquín from Zaragoza came up with his brother, and read his letter aloud, the one he had kept for thirty years; when he finished, his brother hugged him in front of everyone and people applauded for a whole minute. The woman from Valencia, the one with letter number two hundred, came up with her daughter. She didn't read anything. She only said she was glad her daughter was there, beside her, and that was all she wanted to say.

Then there was a moment when nobody moved. Inés looked towards the door, as if expecting someone. And in the doorway appeared a twelve-year-old boy, in a Real Zaragoza shirt and holding a folded sheet of paper, hand in hand with a tall, dark-haired man with the big hands of someone who works with his hands. It was the boy from Teruel. And the man was his father. Ecaterina put her hand to her mouth. Inés had written to the boy, as to everyone, and his grandmother had replied that they would come. What nobody knew, not even Inés, was that the father had come back from Germany in March. Not for a few weeks. For good.

The boy stepped up alone. He was so nervous the paper shook. He read his letter, the same one Ecaterina had found one night in Triana, written in pencil on a page from an exercise book. When he reached the last sentence, "I think he's coming back a bit earlier because I wrote to him", he stopped. He looked at his father, who was standing at the back, next to the lamp. And he added, without reading, a sentence that wasn't in the letter: "And he came back. And he isn't leaving any more." The father couldn't hold back. He covered his face with his hands, there, in front of sixty strangers and a lit lamp. People didn't applaud. For a few seconds, in El Mostrador, all you could hear was the street.

Then Inés asked Ecaterina to read the end of the introduction. Ecaterina stood up. She had such a big lump in her throat that at first her voice wouldn't come out. Ana, from the front row, nodded to her. Ecaterina began: "Today, in a village in Teruel, a boy is waiting for his father." She stopped. She looked at the boy and his father, who were now standing together by the lamp. And she changed the text aloud, in front of everyone: "Today, in a café in Madrid, a boy is no longer waiting for his father, because his father is beside him." She read on to the end. When she finished, the whole of El Mostrador stood up.

Marta spoke next, about "La librera de Triana". She spoke briefly, because, as she said, the real bookseller was in the third row and she didn't dare tell her life story in front of her. Doña Remedios told her aloud to go ahead, that that was what she had given her permission for. Marta read the wedding chapter: the priest who arrived late, the shoes under the pew, the rings in the guitar case. People laughed at the right moments. Faustino, in the third row, next to doña Remedios, discreetly took off his shoes during the reading, as a tribute, and the whole of El Mostrador saw it. Curro, at the back, took out his guitar and played a few bars of sevillanas when Marta finished.

At the end, Andrei put Costel's video on Lola's screen, the one she used for football matches. It showed Costel in the garden of the school in Valencia, surrounded by four teenagers, with the ten-centimetre walnut tree in front of him and the green sign behind. He said, in Spanish, looking at the camera with the face of someone who is a bundle of nerves: "Good evening from Valencia. I'm sorry I'm not there. I'm very glad you're all together. This is Gheorghe's walnut tree. It has five leaves. In ten years it will produce walnuts. When it does, I'll send some to all of you. Come on, a big hug." Álex, beside him, said: "¡Qué pasada!" People laughed and applauded. Rosa Elena filmed it all.

The signing lasted until eleven at night. Ecaterina didn't sign a single book. She refused. She said that book had to be signed by its authors. So the forty-three who had come sat at El Mostrador's tables and signed, side by side, the copies of the people in the queue. Each one signed on the page of their own letter. Some copies ended up with twenty different signatures. Joaquín signed with his brother on the same page. The boy from Teruel signed with his father. The woman from Valencia signed with her daughter. Lola, behind the counter, served coffees and cried at the same time, and said she had never seen so many writers together in such a small café.

Rosa Elena, who had been filming with her camera for four hours without complaining, went up to Ecaterina at a quarter to eleven and asked her why she wasn't signing. Ecaterina explained that it was because that book wasn't hers. The girl thought for a moment. Then she took out of her backpack a copy Inés had given her that afternoon, opened it at the last page of the introduction, where Ecaterina's name appeared in small print, and handed her a pencil. She told her that, in that case, she should sign only there, on her own page, like everyone else. Ecaterina looked at her. Then she signed. Underneath, Rosa Elena wrote in her crooked letters: "And Rosa Elena, who filmed it all for Grandpa."

When the last reader had gone, well after midnight, Lola started tidying up. While wiping the small table under the lamp, she found an envelope that hadn't been there at the start of the evening. It was an old, yellowed envelope, with no stamp, with a Sarajevo address handwritten and crossed out. On top, in a small, cramped hand that Lola knew from the notes on the photos, someone had written a single line: "For Lola. Leave it here. B." Lola didn't open it. She showed it to Ecaterina, who was still there, helping to stack the chairs. Ecaterina recognised the handwriting instantly. The two of them sat down at the back table, with the envelope in front of them.

Inside the envelope was another sheet of paper, newer, folded in four. It was a note for Lola. Ecaterina read it aloud to her, slowly. Begoña said that, thirty years earlier, she had written a letter to a fellow photographer who had stayed in Sarajevo when she came back to Madrid. That she had never sent it, because she was afraid he wouldn't read it. That this evening, listening to other people's letters, she had felt ashamed that she, who spent her life telling others not to be afraid, had been so afraid herself. That she could no longer send it, because he had died in 2003. But that she was glad that at least a lit lamp had it. And it ended: "Not bad. B."

Lola put Begoña's letter on the back shelf, under the lamp, between the Spanish book and the Romanian one, closed, unread. She said that letter wasn't for reading, but for keeping, that there were letters like that. Ecaterina nodded. She thought of her own drawer in Bucharest, of the two letters that had said no, kept next to doña Remedios's bookmark. She thought that every letter eventually found its place, even if it took thirty or forty years. Lola switched off the café lights, all except the lamp. Ecaterina put on her coat. On calle de las Huertas there were still rose petals on the ground and people strolling with books under their arms.

On Saturday morning, before everyone went home, they all went to the Retiro. Doña Remedios wanted to get into a rowing boat on the lake again, as she had in May the year before, and this time Faustino rowed, very slowly, in his red beret, with Rosa Elena sitting between them. The girl asked doña Remedios whether she had enjoyed the party the night before. Doña Remedios told her she had enjoyed it so much that she was still beside herself with joy. Rosa Elena didn't understand the expression. Doña Remedios explained it to her: that the joy was so big it couldn't fit inside a person as small as her. Rosa Elena said that, in that case, the same thing was happening to her.

A week later a handwritten letter for Ecaterina arrived in Bucharest, postmarked Teruel. It had been written by the boy's father. It was short, with spelling mistakes that Ecaterina didn't correct. He told her he had been working for fifteen years at a car factory in Germany, that he came home twice a year and had missed almost all of his son's childhood. That the boy's letter had reached him in September, and that he had read it forty times in the factory canteen. That in March he had quit his job and come back. And that he didn't know how to thank her for putting that letter in a book, because now his son was a writer, and he, at last, was a father.

Two days later, back in Bucharest, Rosa Elena took the video to the village. They watched it on the porch on Sunday afternoon, on Mihai's laptop, with the oil lamp lit although it was still daylight, because Grandpa had said some things had to be watched with the lamp lit. It lasted four hours. Grandpa watched all of it, without getting up, with his glasses on. This time it wasn't just the ceiling: Rosa Elena had filmed everything properly, with the camera steady. When the boy from Teruel appeared with his father, Grandpa asked them to pause the video. He looked at the frozen image for a long time. Then he said, in Romanian, that the boy had done the hardest thing in the world.

Ana asked him what the hardest thing in the world was. Grandpa told her: asking someone to come back. That he had never asked it of anyone, not of his children when they left for the city, nor of his wife when she was in hospital, because he thought asking was a sign of weakness. And that now, at ninety-seven, a twelve-year-old boy had taught him it was the other way round. That the weakness was not asking. Then he asked them to play the video again. When Costel appeared in Valencia with the five-leaf walnut tree, Grandpa laughed so hard his glasses fell off. And when Costel said "venga, un abrazo", Grandpa answered out loud, to the screen: "Venga."
